editorialPolicy: Human-reviewed, time-bounded measurements. Routine automation may flag these entries for review but may not rewrite them.

index.title: By the numbers
index.summary: Four measurements locate the crisis at the military, maritime, and human levels. They are reference points, not a live scorecard.

metrics.label: Missile and drone launches
metrics.detail: Iranian missile and drone launches reported through 1 April.
metrics.context: This measures campaign expenditure, not the size of the surviving inventory.

metrics.label: Gulf oil exports in June
metrics.detail: Exports including bypass routes, against a 24 mb/d prewar average.
metrics.context: A large recovery still left a material gap before renewed July escalation.

metrics.label: Civilian deaths documented
metrics.detail: At least 3,375 deaths and 32,314 injuries in OCHA's fourth update.
metrics.context: The cutoff is early May and the compilation partly relies on Iranian authorities.

metrics.label: Enriched uranium stockpile
metrics.detail: The IAEA cannot verify the present size, composition, or location of the stockpile.
metrics.context: Physical damage cannot substitute for inspection access, records, and material accounting.

consensus.label: Expert consensus
consensus.title: Iran has been badly damaged; the political problem remains open.
consensus.copy: CSIS and RAND describe severe conventional degradation. Chatham House and RUSI agree that military access and physical passage do not by themselves settle war aims, nuclear verification, or commercial confidence.

disagreement.label: Where they disagree
disagreement.title: How much operational success can be converted into a durable outcome.
disagreement.copy: The central dispute is not whether Iran lost major capabilities. It is whether recurring strikes can prevent reconstitution and compel terms, or instead produce a long cycle of attrition, temporary pauses, and renewed escalation.

index.note: Figures are dated to their source cutoff. Missing current access or inventory data is shown as uncertainty, never converted into a zero.

iran-military.title: By the numbers
iran-military.summary: The strongest public evidence shows catastrophic damage to conventional forces alongside a large, poorly measured residual strike and littoral threat.

metrics.label: Conventional surface fleet lost
metrics.detail: Satellite imagery reviewed by CSIS indicates the loss of nearly all conventional gray-hull surface combatants.
metrics.context: This does not include every small craft, mine, coastal missile, drone, or undersea capability.

metrics.label: Missile and drone launches
metrics.detail: Combined launches reported through 1 April.
metrics.context: Expenditure reveals sustained output; it does not reveal the remaining stockpile by subtraction.

metrics.label: Reported stocks retained
metrics.detail: U.S. estimates cited by CSIS put retained missile stocks at 70% and drone stocks at 40%.
metrics.context: These are attributed government estimates, not independently verified inventory counts.

metrics.label: Bushehr harbor basin destroyed
metrics.detail: CSIS estimates that roughly two-fifths of the naval base's harbor basin was destroyed.
metrics.context: Port damage constrains operations and repair, but does not measure every surviving coastal system.

consensus.label: Expert consensus
consensus.title: Severe conventional degradation is real; complete disarmament is not established.
consensus.copy: CSIS and RAND converge on a badly damaged navy and sharply reduced launch tempo. Both also warn that dispersed missile, drone, mine, small-craft, and production knowledge can survive or be rebuilt.

disagreement.label: Where they disagree
disagreement.title: The residual inventory and the speed of reconstitution.
disagreement.copy: Public estimates of launchers, stocks, and production damage vary widely. The hardened and underground portions of the force remain the least observable, making precise remaining-capability percentages especially fragile.

iran-military.note: Fleet language refers to conventional gray-hull surface vessels. It must not be generalized to Iran's entire maritime threat.

forces.title: By the numbers
forces.summary: The force balance is conventionally lopsided, but the exposure is region-wide and measured as much in disrupted trade and civilian systems as in platforms.

metrics.label: Projectiles fired at Gulf states
metrics.detail: Iranian missiles and drones directed at all six GCC states by 19 March.
metrics.context: The count establishes theater-wide exposure, not a uniform level of damage in every state.

metrics.label: GCC states attacked
metrics.detail: Every Gulf Cooperation Council member was exposed to Iranian attack.
metrics.context: Geographic reach complicates basing, interception, logistics, and regional diplomacy.

metrics.label: Gulf oil exports in June
metrics.detail: Exports including bypass routes recovered from the shock but remained below the 24 mb/d prewar average.
metrics.context: Commercial recovery depends on shipping, insurance, ports, crews, and political restraint—not naval access alone.

metrics.label: Food-import exposure
metrics.detail: The share of Gulf food imports reported as moving through the Strait of Hormuz.
metrics.context: This is a vulnerability measure cited by Carnegie from Reuters reporting, not a measured loss rate.

consensus.label: Expert consensus
consensus.title: U.S. and Israeli high-end dominance coexists with persistent regional vulnerability.
consensus.copy: Air and naval superiority can suppress major formations and protect selected nodes. It cannot eliminate every cheap projectile, coastal system, logistics disruption, or political cost imposed across six exposed Gulf states.

disagreement.label: Where they disagree
disagreement.title: Whether deeper U.S.-led integration or greater Gulf autonomy is the safer long-term answer.
disagreement.copy: Some analysis emphasizes integrated defenses and sustained U.S. presence. Gulf policy also reflects fear of entrapment, pressure to diversify security relationships, and a preference for negotiated restraint.

forces.note: Projectile totals measure attempts across the theater; they are not interchangeable with impact, interception, or damage counts.

diplomatic.title: By the numbers
diplomatic.summary: The most consequential numbers on the nuclear file are dated baselines. The present inventory and activity cannot be responsibly reduced to a current total.

metrics.label: Last-accounted 60% stockpile
metrics.detail: The IAEA's last public accounting of uranium enriched up to 60%.
metrics.context: This is a pre-loss-of-access snapshot, not a current verified quantity.

metrics.label: Declared enrichment facilities
metrics.detail: Declared facilities whose present status cannot be fully verified.
metrics.context: Declarations and visible damage do not answer where all material, records, equipment, and personnel are now.

metrics.label: Theoretical bomb equivalents
metrics.detail: A rough weapons-equivalent calculation if the last-accounted stock were further enriched and weaponized.
metrics.context: It does not mean Iran possesses ten weapons, warheads, or a demonstrated weaponization chain.

metrics.label: Pickaxe Mountain
metrics.detail: The deeply buried complex has not been inspected by the IAEA and its contents remain unknown.
metrics.context: Continued excavation is observable; nuclear material or activity at the site is not established.

consensus.label: Expert consensus
consensus.title: Bombing cannot recreate safeguards knowledge.
consensus.copy: Specialists broadly agree that physical damage may delay activity but cannot establish where material is, what equipment survived, or whether expertise has dispersed. Any durable bargain needs inspection access and an accounting process.

disagreement.label: Where they disagree
disagreement.title: Whether only zero enrichment is stable—or whether bounded enrichment can be verified.
disagreement.copy: The argument turns on acceptable residual capability, the sequence of sanctions and strike relief, and whether inspections can become credible before each side gives up its principal leverage.

diplomatic.note: Nuclear quantities are deliberately labeled by accounting date. The report does not treat theoretical weapon equivalents as actual bombs.

inside-iran.title: By the numbers
inside-iran.summary: The humanitarian picture is severe and still incomplete. The best public figures are dated snapshots assembled under restricted access.

metrics.label: Civilian deaths documented
metrics.detail: At least 3,375 deaths and 32,314 injuries in OCHA's fourth humanitarian update.
metrics.context: The cutoff is early May; the total should not be presented as a current cumulative count.

metrics.label: Civilian units damaged
metrics.detail: Homes and other civilian units reported damaged by 1 April.
metrics.context: OCHA also reported 763 damaged schools in the same early-war snapshot.

metrics.label: National internet blackout
metrics.detail: The shutdown cut roughly 90 million people off from normal access for most of 2026.
metrics.context: Connectivity controls obscure civilian conditions, political attitudes, and the scale of dissent.

metrics.label: Health centers / hospitals damaged
metrics.detail: Estimated health centers and hospitals damaged, alongside pharmaceutical and emergency-service losses.
metrics.context: Facility damage compounds staff, supply, access, power, and communications failures.

consensus.label: Expert consensus
consensus.title: The state remains functional, but the civilian burden and information darkness are profound.
consensus.copy: Humanitarian reporting supports large-scale harm to people, housing, schools, and health systems. Political analysis also cautions that repression and communications controls make both regime resilience and public opposition difficult to measure.

disagreement.label: Where they disagree
disagreement.title: Whether wartime centralization signals durable resilience or accumulating brittleness.
disagreement.copy: Order can coexist with hollowed services, fear, elite distrust, and latent dissent. Public evidence does not yet establish which pressures are approaching a political threshold.

inside-iran.note: Humanitarian totals are source-cutoff snapshots. Restricted access and damaged communications make later nationwide totals especially uncertain.

reactions.title: By the numbers
reactions.summary: Regional reactions are best understood through exposure: attacks reached every Gulf state, while trade and food systems remained dependent on a commercially trusted Hormuz.

metrics.label: Projectiles directed at the GCC
metrics.detail: Missiles and drones fired toward all six GCC states by 19 March.
metrics.context: The geographic spread helps explain why Gulf governments seek both protection and de-escalation.

metrics.label: GCC members exposed
metrics.detail: The conflict reached every member of the Gulf Cooperation Council.
metrics.context: Shared exposure has not produced identical preferences on basing, retaliation, or diplomacy.

metrics.label: June / prewar Gulf exports
metrics.detail: Million barrels per day exported in June versus the prewar average.
metrics.context: The gap captures only oil volume, not all shipping, insurance, product, and food-system effects.

metrics.label: Food imports routed through Hormuz
metrics.detail: Reported share of Gulf food imports exposed to the waterway.
metrics.context: This structural dependence shapes restraint even where military protection is strong.

consensus.label: Expert consensus
consensus.title: Gulf states want defense without permanent entrapment.
consensus.copy: Their exposure to projectiles and shipping disruption makes U.S. protection important. The same exposure raises the cost of open-ended escalation and gives Gulf governments strong incentives to preserve mediation channels.

disagreement.label: Where they disagree
disagreement.title: What security architecture should follow the war.
disagreement.copy: Positions diverge over deeper U.S. integration, regional self-reliance, relations with China, and whether accommodation with Iran is a stabilizing necessity or a source of renewed risk.

reactions.note: Regional positions are inferred from stated policy and observable exposure, not from treating the GCC as a single political actor.

analysis.title: By the numbers
analysis.summary: The core evidence supports a paradox: overwhelming operational access, persistent Iranian capacity to impose cost, and no demonstrated mechanism for political closure.

metrics.label: First-week launch-tempo change
metrics.detail: RAND reports a fall from more than 400 launches on day one to roughly 20–40 per day.
metrics.context: A reduced tempo demonstrates suppression; it does not establish exhausted stocks or political capitulation.

metrics.label: Conventional surface fleet lost
metrics.detail: CSIS imagery analysis finds catastrophic losses among conventional surface combatants.
metrics.context: The residual littoral threat still includes systems outside the gray-hull fleet.

metrics.label: June export recovery
metrics.detail: Gulf oil exports reached about two-thirds of the 24 mb/d prewar average.
metrics.context: Recovery remained incomplete and depended on more than physical navigation.

metrics.label: Deaths / injuries documented
metrics.detail: OCHA's fourth update records the minimum civilian toll through its early-May cutoff.
metrics.context: The political result cannot be assessed without the human cost and the limits of wartime reporting.

consensus.label: Expert consensus
consensus.title: Operational dominance and strategic success are different questions.
consensus.copy: CSIS and RAND see substantial military effects. Chatham House and RUSI stress that war termination, commercial normalization, nuclear verification, and political legitimacy require mechanisms that strike access alone does not supply.

disagreement.label: Where they disagree
disagreement.title: Whether continued pressure improves bargaining leverage or locks in attrition.
disagreement.copy: One view treats repeated degradation and reconstitution denial as a path to better terms. The other expects temporary ceasefires, adaptive rebuilding, and recurring escalation unless the political objectives are narrowed.

analysis.note: This section maps analytical convergence and divergence. Belligerent estimates remain attributed even when cited by a research institution.

scenarios.title: How the outlook is measured
scenarios.summary: The scenario set is an indicator system, not a prediction market. It shows what evidence would move the picture and what remains unknowable.

metrics.label: Conditional pathways
metrics.detail: Armed pause, negotiated settlement, managed transition, democratic transition, and chaotic fragmentation.
metrics.context: The pathways are mechanisms, not mutually precise forecast buckets.

metrics.label: Discriminating systems
metrics.detail: Strike tempo, commercial shipping, nuclear access, and elite cohesion.
metrics.context: Movement in these systems matters more than rhetoric or single-day noise.

metrics.label: Primary review horizon
metrics.detail: A bounded window for watching mechanisms and leading indicators.
metrics.context: Longer-term outcomes remain path-dependent and should not inherit short-term confidence.

metrics.label: Unsupported probabilities
metrics.detail: The report does not assign precise likelihoods without a defensible model and calibrated dataset.
metrics.context: Qualitative ordering is kept separate from numerical probability.

consensus.label: Shared analytical baseline
consensus.title: An armed pause is easier to reach than a durable settlement.
consensus.copy: The hardest issues—verification, sanctions, maritime restraint, security guarantees, reconstitution, and Iran's internal order—can be deferred by a pause but not resolved by one.

disagreement.label: Key forecast dispute
disagreement.title: Whether pressure produces negotiation, adaptation, or political fracture.
disagreement.copy: Analysts differ on which mechanism dominates. The report therefore follows indicators for each pathway rather than forcing uncertainty into a single percentage.

scenarios.note: Scenario labels describe conditional mechanisms. They should change only when the underlying mechanism or evidence changes.

opposition.title: By the numbers
opposition.summary: The measurable opposition picture is mostly diaspora mobilization, organizational formation, and information restriction—not representative support inside Iran.

metrics.label: Munich rally estimate
metrics.detail: Police estimate for a large diaspora opposition rally associated with Reza Pahlavi.
metrics.context: Large diaspora turnout demonstrates mobilization abroad, not a representative mandate inside Iran.

metrics.label: Toronto rally estimate
metrics.detail: Police estimate for a second very large diaspora gathering.
metrics.context: The figure is evidence of diaspora reach and organization, not internal electoral support.

metrics.label: Kurdish groups in coalition
metrics.detail: Five Iranian Kurdish organizations announced a coalition amid wider opposition tensions.
metrics.context: Coordination within one political field does not resolve disputes over leadership or territorial order.

metrics.label: Current support inside Iran
metrics.detail: There is no reliable, representative current measure of support for Pahlavi or any opposition bloc inside Iran.
metrics.context: Repression, war, displacement, and the 88-day blackout make confident ranking especially hazardous.

consensus.label: Expert consensus
consensus.title: Visibility is not legitimacy, and opposition is not institutional readiness.
consensus.copy: Reza Pahlavi is consequential and capable of mobilizing large diaspora audiences. Iran's opposition nevertheless remains plural, divided over leadership and intervention, and without a demonstrated nationwide mandate or transition apparatus.

disagreement.label: Where they disagree
disagreement.title: Pahlavi's internal support and the effect of foreign military pressure.
disagreement.copy: Supporters see a focal point for transition; critics see an externally amplified figure whose reach inside Iran is unproven. Analysts also disagree on whether war weakens the state politically or strengthens coercive nationalism.

opposition.note: Diaspora attendance and coalition counts are observable. Internal popularity, organizational depth, and transition legitimacy remain separate questions.

background.title: The numbers that shaped the bargain
background.summary: The 2015 agreement's core logic was measurable constraint plus verification. Its collapse removed both the limits and the shared baseline.

metrics.label: JCPOA enriched-stock limit
metrics.detail: The cap on Iran's enriched-uranium stockpile under the 2015 agreement.
metrics.context: The limit worked with monitoring and other restrictions; it was not a standalone guarantee.

metrics.label: JCPOA enrichment ceiling
metrics.detail: The permitted enrichment level under the deal.
metrics.context: The ceiling was designed to lengthen the time needed to produce weapons-grade material.

metrics.label: Enrichment-capacity reduction
metrics.detail: Approximate reduction required under the agreement.
metrics.context: Constraint was paired with verification and sanctions relief in a reciprocal structure.

metrics.label: Target breakout time
metrics.detail: The agreement's intended minimum period for producing enough weapons-grade material for one device.
metrics.context: Breakout time is a material-production estimate, not the time to build and deploy a weapon.

consensus.label: Expert consensus
consensus.title: The JCPOA bought time and visibility; it did not settle the wider conflict.
consensus.copy: Its numerical limits and inspections constrained the nuclear program. It did not resolve missiles, regional deterrence, domestic repression, or the durability of sanctions relief.

disagreement.label: Where they disagree
disagreement.title: Whether a narrow nuclear bargain can still be insulated from the regional war.
disagreement.copy: One view treats nuclear constraint as a separable, urgent transaction. Another argues that sanctions, missiles, maritime security, and regional guarantees must now be negotiated together.

background.note: Historical baselines are retained because they show what was once measurable. They are not descriptions of Iran's present nuclear position.

sources.title: Four rules for reading the report
sources.summary: The source page keeps methodology visible without turning the reader experience into an update dashboard.

metrics.label: One evidentiary burden
metrics.detail: Each consequential factual claim must point to the source that actually supports it.
metrics.context: A nearby link does not count if it supports only the general topic.

metrics.label: Fact, assessment, forecast
metrics.detail: Observable claims, analytical judgments, and conditional futures are kept visibly distinct.
metrics.context: Confidence language must match the mode.

metrics.label: Unknown remaining inventory
metrics.detail: Launches and known losses are not subtracted from an uncertain starting stock to invent a current total.
metrics.context: Dated institutional estimates remain attributed.

metrics.label: Every fragile number
metrics.detail: Casualties, traffic, prices, deployments, and inventories retain their source cutoff.
metrics.context: A stale but well-labeled baseline is safer than false current precision.

consensus.label: Editorial standard
consensus.title: The reader should be able to tell what is known, inferred, and still contested.
consensus.copy: Primary records establish baselines; independent reporting verifies events; specialist institutions supply analysis. None of those roles is interchangeable.

disagreement.label: Required disclosure
disagreement.title: Serious sources often disagree because they answer different questions.
disagreement.copy: The report maps those disagreements instead of averaging them away. Belligerent claims, imagery estimates, humanitarian compilations, and policy arguments keep their provenance and limits.

sources.note: Routine automation may update the compact latest feed. Standing synthesis and this evidence desk require human review.
